South Ribble's population increased by around 2,000 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 110,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of South Ribble increased by 1.8%, from around 109,100 in 2011 to around 111,000 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the North West (5.2%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, South Ribble was home to around 7.0 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 6.9 in 2011. This area was close to the median population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in South Ribble than across the North West

An older South Ribble

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of South Ribble increased by two years, from 42 to 44 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the North West as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by just under 2,400 (an increase of 11.0%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 3,600 (14.9% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.8 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Family in South Ribble

South Ribble saw England's joint third-largest percentage-point fall (alongside Burnley and Sunderland) in the proportion of households including a couple with only non-dependent children (from 7.7% in 2011 to 7.0% in 2021).

England's largest decreases in the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children occurred in Isles of Scilly (from 4.8% to 2.2%) followed by North East Derbyshire (from 7.8% to 6.9%).

Because of its small size, comparisons to Isles of Scilly should be made with caution.

Despite the decrease, South Ribble was in the highest 25% of English local authority areas for the share of households including a couple with only non-dependent children in 2021.

The percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children in South Ribble decreased by 0.7 percentage points

Changing relationships in South Ribble

South Ribble saw the North West's third-largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 9.2% in 2011 to 10.1% in 2021).

Across the region, only Wyre (from 9.9% to 10.9%) and Fylde (from 10.4% to 11.3%) saw a greater increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership.

Across the North West, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership fell from 9.3% to 9.1%, while the percentage in nearby Chorley increased from 10.0% to 10.4%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in South Ribble increased by 0.8 percentage points

Disability in South Ribble

South Ribble saw the North West's third-largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 9.8% in 2011 to 10.6% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Across the region, only Lancaster (from 10.7% to 11.7%) and Wirral (from 10.7% to 11.6%) saw a greater increase in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little.

Across the North West, the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little remained 10.7%, while the proportion in nearby Chorley increased from 10.0% to 10.7%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a little in South Ribble increased by 0.8 percentage points

Rise in private renting

In 2021, 12.8% of South Ribble households rented privately. This figure increased from 9.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 1 in 10 households (10.4%) lived in socially rented housing, compared with 10.5% in 2011. The percentage of South Ribble households that owned their home (outright or with a mortgage or loan) decreased from 78.8% to 76.0%.

This area had the region’s third lowest percentage of privately-rented homes. Across the region, only Copeland (11.0%) and Allerdale (12.2%) had a lower percentage of privately-rented homes.

Private renting in South Ribble increased by 3.5 percentage points

Unpaid care in South Ribble

In 2021, 5.1% of South Ribble residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.8% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

This area had the region’s joint highest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (alongside Wyre and St. Helens). Wirral had the North West's next highest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (5.0%), while Manchester had the region's lowest proportion (3.4%).

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in South Ribble decreased by 2.7 percentage points

Religion in South Ribble

In 2021, 30.8% of South Ribble residents reported having "No religion", up from 17.0% in 2011. The rise of 13.9 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in South Ribble. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North West, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 19.8% to 32.6%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 61.8% of people in South Ribble described themselves as Christian (down from 75.7%), while 5.0% did not state their religion (down from 5.7% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 30.8% of usual residents in South Ribble reported having "No religion"

South Ribble residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 102,600 South Ribble residents said they were born in England. This represented 92.4% of the local population. The figure has risen from just over 101,800 in 2011, which at the time represented 93.4% of South Ribble's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 1,700 South Ribble residents reporting this country of birth (1.5%). This figure was down from just over 1,800 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.7% of the population of South Ribble.

The number of South Ribble residents born in Poland rose from around 450 in 2011 (0.4% of the local population) to just under 750 in 2021 (0.7%).

In 2021, 92.4% of South Ribble residents reported their country of birth as England

People looking after their family or home in South Ribble

In 2021, 2.8% of South Ribble residents (aged 16 years and over) said they were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home. This figure increased from 2.4% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 6 in 10 people (58.3%) said they were employed (excluding full-time students), compared with 60.7% in 2011. The percentage of South Ribble residents who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) decreased from 2.7% to 1.8%.

This area had the region’s third lowest percentage of people who were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home. Across the region, only Ribble Valley (2.4%) and South Lakeland (2.6%) had a lower percentage of people who were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were looking after their family or home (economically inactive) in South Ribble increased by 0.4 percentage points

Working hours in South Ribble

In 2021, 8.4% of South Ribble residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (8.5%).

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.9%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 10.9% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 61.2% to 63.3%.

South Ribble saw the North West's joint third-largest fall (alongside Copeland) in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week. This area had the region’s eighth lowest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in South Ribble decreased by 0.1 percentage points

National identity in South Ribble

In 2021, 2.5% of South Ribble residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 1.8% in 2011.

In 2021, 0.7% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.2% in 2011. The percentage of residents in South Ribble that identified as "British only" increased from 14.4% to 58.9%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the North West (2.3 percentage points, from 4.7% to 7.1%) than in South Ribble (0.7 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in South Ribble increased by 0.7 percentage points

Health in South Ribble

In 2021, 48.9% of South Ribble residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 46.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.3% to 33.8%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of South Ribble residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.0% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.3% to 3.7%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in South Ribble increased by 2.0 percentage points

Ethnic groups in South Ribble

In 2021, 2.1% of South Ribble residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 1.5% in 2011. The 0.6 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North West, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 6.2% to 8.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 95.4% of people in South Ribble identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.1% in 2011), while 1.7% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.1% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category increased from 0.2% in 2011 to 0.5% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
